attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post, stated as his view.

semantics.note: Unhedged present-tense claim about the state of alignment research. The normalisation matches the statement.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair: robust, general alignment was unresolved. It correctly treats 'remotely' as emphasis rather than a denial of all progress. The early-2024 window is a reasonable reading of the present tense.

evidence.note: January 2024 primary research. Standard safety training failed to remove deceptive behaviour that was deliberately implanted. The failures were induced in experiments, not seen in deployment, but they show a substantial robustness gap.
A 2022 OpenAI disclosure that no scalable solution was known. It predates the window, so it is background only.
A December 2023 OpenAI report of progress on weak-to-strong supervision, with stated limits. It shows some progress but no general solution, and it is just before the window.

reviews.rationale: Primary research from the window (e1) found that standard safety methods failed against deliberately deceptive models. Nothing in the packet shows a general, validated alignment method. The progress OpenAI reported (e3) came with explicit limits and does not meet the contradiction condition. The support condition is met under a fair plain reading.

attribution.note: Marcus is describing OpenAI's position in his own words, and the characterisation is his. He is not quoting OpenAI.

semantics.note: The core claim is a historical one about what OpenAI argued. 'Would crush' describes the hypothetical effect of the exemption; it is not a dated forecast.

contract.note: The contract turns 'would crush' into a harm prediction that must be proven before the claim can be supported. Marcus named no exemption, deadline or jurisdiction, so that bar cannot be met. Whether 'exemption' covers fair use is also an interpretation he did not supply.

evidence.note: OpenAI's December 2023 submission to the UK House of Lords, read from a mirrored copy. It says training leading models is impossible without copyrighted material, while also saying the law permits it. This partly supports the attribution and says nothing about harm.
OpenAI's January 2024 post calls fair use for training 'necessary for innovators'. This supports the attribution only and says nothing on harm to creators.

reviews.rationale: In substance, the attribution holds. OpenAI said it could not train leading models without copyrighted material and called fair use necessary, although it framed this as existing law rather than a new exemption. The contract also requires proof of severe harm to creators from an unspecified exemption. The packet has none, and the contract says missing harm evidence is not a contradiction. The compound claim therefore stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his own post.

semantics.note: An unhedged present-tense claim that OpenAI absorbs essentially none of the externalities. The normalisation is faithful. The claim about three authors he knows is reasonably set aside.

contract.note: Reading the claim as 'a negligible share of harm costs' is ordinary. Separating prevention from compensation is defensible. The two-month window is inferred but reasonable for a present-tense claim.

evidence.note: The November 2023 Copyright Shield commitment covers customers' copyright litigation costs. It predates the window, is a commitment rather than reported payments, and has a narrow scope.
OpenAI's January 2024 election post describes efforts to prevent misuse. That is prevention, not compensation, and the post gives no amounts.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no estimate of the external harm attributable to OpenAI and no record of costs it actually bore in the window. Neither the support nor the contradiction condition can be checked. The company items show prevention efforts and a narrow commitment, not a material share of harm costs. Lack of disclosure cannot prove zero spending.
